title: The Sharpe Pint: Reopening Hormuz, SpaceX's Orbit, and the Sins of Financial LLMs

opening_mood.text: Morning. If you spent your weekend ignoring your work phone, congratulations—you missed about a decade's worth of market history compressed into 48 hours. We have a sudden geopolitical breakthrough in the Middle East, the biggest IPO in human history, and a central bank triple-threat week that is going to test Kevin Warsh's tightrope-walking skills on day one.
Grab a coffee (or something stronger if you are holding short energy positions). Here is what you actually need to know to look like the smartest person in the room today.

content.text: Peace in our time (or at least 60 days of it): US and Iran strike a deal

On Sunday night, President Trump announced that a deal with Iran is "now complete," authorising the immediate, toll-free reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. While the official signing ceremony is set for Friday in Switzerland, the market did not wait for the ink to dry. Brent crude tumbled over 4.5% to around $83 a barrel, and global equity markets went into orbit. Japan's Nikkei surged 5%, South Korea's Kospi jumped over 5.2%, and US stock futures popped.

The deal establishes a 60-day ceasefire and temporary sanctions relief for Iranian oil exports while negotiators hammer out the technical details of Iran's nuclear programme. For a global economy that has been choked by shipping blockages—with nearly 600 vessels currently waiting to exit the Strait—this is a massive relief valve.

The City Angle: Macro desks are aggressively unwinding geopolitical risk premiums. While energy stocks are taking a beating, the broader "risk-on" melt-up is the dominant trade. The big question now is how this impacts the Federal Reserve's interest rate decision this week. Falling oil prices will cool headline inflation, giving the Fed the perfect cover to cut rates if they want to bow to political pressure.

What to say at the pub: "Reopening the Strait of Hormuz is a massive supply-side win, but the real trade is the Fed. If oil stays down, it gives them the perfect excuse to cut rates into an already euphoric market. Get ready for a proper summer melt-up."
To the moon: SpaceX smashes records in historic $1.77tn market debut

On Friday, Elon Musk's SpaceX officially transitioned from a private playground to the public markets, debuting under the ticker SPCX. Priced at $135 a share, the company was valued at a staggering $1.77 trillion. By the closing bell, the stock had surged over 19% to finish at $161.11, pushing its market cap past $2.1 trillion and officially minting Elon Musk as the world's first trillionaire.

The scale of the debut is hard to comprehend. Retail investors placed over $100 billion in orders, and institutional heavyweights like BlackRock threw down $5 billion on their own. To keep the momentum going, MSCI immediately added the stock to its Standard and Large-Cap Indexes, triggering massive, non-discretionary buying from passive funds.

The City Angle: This is a generational liquidity event that completely reshapes global equity indices. For Equity Capital Markets (ECM) desks, it's the ultimate proof of concept: the mega-IPO is back. For asset managers, the immediate index inclusion means portfolio managers have had to scramble to reallocate capital, likely selling down other tech and semiconductor names to fund their forced SPCX purchases.

What to say in an interview: "The SpaceX IPO is a watershed moment for ECM. If a company can list at $1.77 trillion and still pop nearly 20% on day one, it proves there is an enormous mountain of institutional cash waiting for high-quality mega-caps. Expect a flood of late-stage private tech firms to dust off their S-1 filings this quarter."
Fox tunes into streaming with a $22bn Roku buyout

Fox Corporation is making its biggest streaming bet yet, announcing a definitive agreement to acquire connected-TV pioneer Roku in a cash-and-stock deal valued at $22 billion. Fox is paying $160 per share ($96 in cash and 0.9693 shares of Fox Class A stock), representing a premium that sent Roku shares up in premarket trading, while Fox shares dipped as investors digested the debt load.

The deal combines Fox's powerhouse live sports and news portfolio (and its ad-supported streaming service, Tubi) with Roku's platform, which reaches over 100 million global households. On a pro forma basis, the combined entity will become the third-largest player in US television by viewing share.

The City Angle: This is a classic "content meets pipes" consolidation play, but with a modern twist: first-party data. Fox isn't just buying a streaming box; they are buying direct access to the viewing habits and ad-targeting data of half the broadband homes in America. To fund the cash portion, Fox has secured a massive $12 billion bridge loan from Morgan Stanley, which will test the debt markets' appetite for media consolidation.

What to say at work: "Fox buying Roku is all about the FAST (Free Ad-Supported Streaming TV) ecosystem. By pairing Tubi's content with Roku's hardware footprint and first-party data, Fox is bypassing the traditional cable bundle entirely and building a highly monetisable, closed-loop advertising machine."
Green light in Washington: DOJ approves $111bn Paramount-WBD merger

Late on Friday, the US Department of Justice's antitrust division officially closed its investigation into Paramount Skydance's acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, clearing the $111 billion mega-merger with absolutely no conditions. The DOJ concluded that the tie-up would actually "increase competition" by creating a more robust alternative to dominant tech platforms like Netflix and Apple.

The deal, heavily bankrolled by Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison (who provided a $40 billion personal guarantee), will bring CBS News and CNN under common ownership and combine the massive libraries of HBO Max and Paramount+. However, the celebration might be premature: several US state attorneys general are preparing lawsuits to block the deal, and international watchdogs are still circling.

The City Angle: For M&A bankers, this is a clear signal that the US antitrust regime under the current administration is highly permissive of mega-mergers. However, the real battleground now shifts across the Atlantic. The UK's Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has set an August deadline for its own probe, and European regulators are scrutinising the $24 billion in Gulf sovereign wealth fund backing.

What to say in an interview: "While the DOJ's unconditional clearance is a massive win for Paramount-WBD, the deal isn't home safe. The UK's CMA has shown a strong willingness to act as a global antitrust spoiler, and with state AGs preparing to sue, we could see a highly fragmented regulatory outcome."
Gilat buys Comtech's space business in a strategic mid-cap carve-out

On Monday morning, Gilat Satellite Networks announced a definitive agreement to acquire Comtech's Satellite & Space Communications segment for $157.5 million in cash. The transaction will be fully funded from Gilat's existing cash reserves, creating a combined entity with projected annual revenues exceeding $700 million.

For Comtech, the sale is a vital lifeline. The company has been under severe financial strain, recently amending its credit facilities to suspend leverage and interest coverage covenants until mid-2027. For Gilat, the acquisition more than doubles its defense revenues and significantly expands its US manufacturing footprint and RF engineering capabilities.

The City Angle: This is a textbook opportunistic carve-out. In the mid-cap space, balance sheet strength is everything. Gilat is using its net cash position to buy high-quality, mission-critical defense assets from a distressed seller at a highly attractive valuation. It highlights the accelerating consolidation in the satellite ground infrastructure and defense tech markets as global demand for resilient communications surges.

What to say at work: "The Gilat-Comtech deal is a classic example of balance sheet arbitrage. Comtech gets the cash it desperately needs to stave off covenant breaches, while Gilat buys high-value defense tech assets on the cheap. It's a great case study of how mid-cap consolidation is playing out in the defense sector."

sections.title: Markets Briefing: What Moved and Why

content.text: If you fell asleep on Friday afternoon and woke up today, you would be forgiven for thinking you had missed a decade of market history. We have just witnessed the biggest IPO in human history, a sudden geopolitical breakthrough that has sent crude off a cliff, and we are heading straight into a central bank triple-threat week. Global equities are absolutely buzzing. Monday morning saw S&P 500 futures up 1.3 per cent and Nasdaq futures leaping 1.8 per cent, while Asian markets went on an absolute tear: Japan's Nikkei 225 benchmark soared 5.5 per cent and South Korea's Kospi jumped 5.7 per cent.

The primary catalyst for this risk-on party is a tentative peace framework between the US and Iran announced over the weekend. President Trump confirmed the initial agreement and authorised an end to the US naval blockade of Iranian ports, with a formal signing scheduled for Friday in Switzerland. The market reaction was swift and brutal for energy bulls: Brent crude tumbled 4.7 per cent to below 83 dollars a barrel, and WTI crude lost over 5 per cent to slide to 80.53 dollars. This is a massive relief valve for global inflation. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz since March had choked off 20 per cent of the world's oil and LNG, driving Brent up from 72 dollars to over 113 dollars. While this 'peace dividend' is a major psychological win, energy desks warn that shipping and insurance rates will take months to normalise, meaning we are not out of the inflationary woods just yet.

Meanwhile, Elon Musk has officially entered the stratosphere. On Friday, SpaceX made its highly anticipated Nasdaq debut under the ticker SPCX, pulling off a record-shattering 75 billion dollar IPO at 135 dollars a share. The stock did not just launch; it went into orbit, surging 19.2 per cent on its first day of trading to close at 160.95 dollars. That puts SpaceX's market capitalisation at a mind-boggling 2.1 trillion dollars, making it the sixth-largest listed company in the US and officially crowning Musk as the world's first trillionaire with a net worth of 1.1 trillion dollars. For the active managers among us, the real game is index inclusion: Nasdaq has already bent its rules to allow SpaceX to join the Nasdaq-100 after just 15 trading days if it stays in the top 40, triggering massive automatic buying from passive QQQ funds. The S&P 500, however, has refused to fast-track it, setting up a fascinating liquidity tug-of-war.

As if that was not enough action, we are now staring down the barrel of a massive central bank week. The main event is the Federal Reserve's FOMC meeting on 16-17 June. This is the first meeting chaired by Kevin Warsh, who was sworn in on 22 May to replace Jerome Powell. But Powell is not gone; he remains on the Board of Governors with a vote through 2028, earning him the nickname 'shadow chair' on Wall Street. Warsh is caught in a brutal political and economic vice. Trump is publicly demanding rate cuts, but May CPI inflation clocked in at a hot 4.2 per cent and payrolls beat expectations at 172,000. While the Fed is almost certain to hold rates steady at 3.50 to 3.75 per cent this week, the real battle is over the 'easing bias'. Bond markets are still pricing in an 80 per cent chance of a rate hike by year-end, meaning Warsh's first press conference on Wednesday will be a masterclass in tightrope walking.

Finally, do not sleep on the Bank of Japan. On Tuesday, the BoJ is widely expected to hike its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 1.0 per cent—its highest level in 31 years. In a bizarre twist of corporate drama, BoJ Governor Kazuo Ueda was hospitalised last week with a hepatic cyst, meaning the central bank is poised to deliver its most hawkish policy shift in three decades without its chief at the table. If you are trading USD/JPY this week, buckle up; the yen is sitting at 160, and a 1.0 per cent rate could trigger some serious repatriation flows.

sections.title: Financial Idea of the Day: The Alchemy of EBITDA Add-Backs

content.text: If you have spent more than five minutes looking at an information memorandum (IM) or a Quality of Earnings (QofE) report, you will know that 'reported' EBITDA is basically just a starting bid. In the world of M&A and private equity, the real action is in 'Adjusted' or 'Pro-Forma' EBITDA. This is where management teams and sell-side advisors perform financial alchemy, turning cold, hard expenses into 'one-off' adjustments that magically disappear from the cost base.

According to a February 2026 study by S&P Global, EBITDA add-backs now account for an astonishing 29% of adjusted EBITDA in the average sale process. Even more sobering: S&P found that only 8% of companies actually managed to meet or exceed their pre-close projected EBITDA in their first year post-acquisition. The rest missed their leverage targets by a mile, sometimes by over 2.3x. In short, the 'adjustments' are often pure fiction.
How the Magic Works: A Quick Example

Let us say a mid-market widget manufacturer, 'Sloane & Co.', reports a GAAP EBITDA of £10 million. They have £70 million of debt, meaning their leverage is a hefty 7.0x. To make the business look more attractive (and less likely to default), the sell-side bankers construct a 'Quality of Earnings' bridge to show 'Adjusted EBITDA' of £14.5 million. They add back £1.5 million of 'non-recurring' restructuring costs (even though they have restructured every year since 2021), £1.0 million of 'excess' founder compensation (arguing a professional CEO would cost less), and £2.0 million of 'run-rate synergies' from an acquisition they have not actually integrated yet.

Suddenly, Sloane & Co.’s leverage magically drops from 7.0x to 4.8x (£70m / £14.5m). Lenders write the check, the PE sponsor pays a 10x multiple on the £14.5m (£145m EV), and everyone goes to the pub.
Why This Matters in Asset Management and Private Credit

If you are a private credit lender or a high-yield analyst, these add-backs are where you get run over. Credit agreements often allow companies to calculate their leverage covenants using these 'pro-forma' adjusted figures. If the 'synergies' never materialise (and 92% of the time they do not, according to that S&P data), the company's actual leverage is far higher than the covenant suggests. You have effectively lent money to a 7.0x leveraged business on 5.0x terms.
Common Beginner Mistake

Taking 'Adjusted EBITDA' at face value. If a company has 'one-time restructuring charges' or 'system implementation costs' on its income statement for five consecutive years, those are not one-offs. They are recurring capital or operating expenses disguised as adjustments. A good analyst always builds a 'reconciliation of the reconciliation' to strip out the nonsense.
How It Links to Interviews

If you are interviewing for private equity, private credit, or M&A, you will almost certainly get asked: 'How would you assess the quality of a company's EBITDA?' or 'What are the risks of using Adjusted EBITDA in an LBO model?' Your answer should immediately reference the difference between 'hard' add-backs (like a settled, one-time legal dispute or excess owner salary) and 'soft' or 'synthetic' add-backs (like unrealised synergies, future cost savings, or capitalised software development). Mentioning the recent S&P Global data—showing that 92% of companies miss their adjusted EBITDA targets post-close—will make you look incredibly commercially aware.
Over a Pint: What to Say

items: If a company has had 'one-off restructuring costs' every year since the Brexit vote, that is not a restructuring—that is just how they run the business.

The gap between reported and adjusted EBITDA is basically a measure of how creative the sell-side bankers are feeling. When add-backs hit 30% of the total, you are not buying a business; you are buying a PowerPoint presentation.

sections.title: Quant / AI Finance Idea of the Day: Beating the Curse of Dimensionality

content.text: If you have ever sat through a financial engineering lecture, you will know that pricing options on a basket of, say, 100 stocks is the ultimate boss fight of quantitative finance. Traditional numerical methods like finite differences or binomial trees suffer from the 'curse of dimensionality'. If you try to build a 100-dimensional grid, your computer will run out of memory before you even finish defining the first axis. Standard Monte Carlo is great for linear payoffs, but the moment you introduce non-linearities—like different borrowing and lending rates, or counterparty default risk—it completely falls apart because you cannot easily run backward induction on simulated paths.
The Magic Trick: Deep BSDE Solvers

Enter the Deep BSDE (Backward Stochastic Differential Equation) solver, a brilliant marriage of stochastic calculus and deep learning popularised by Weinan E, Jiequn Han, and Arnulf Jentzen. The core mathematical insight is that a high-dimensional parabolic PDE (which describes our option price) can be reformulated as a system of Forward-Backward SDEs. The forward SDE simulates the underlying asset prices moving through time. The backward SDE describes how the option price and its sensitivity (the gradient, or Delta) evolve backwards from the terminal payoff.

To solve this without a grid, we play a game of forward simulation with feedback. We start at today (t=0) with a guess of the option's price (a learnable parameter, Y0) and its initial Delta (Z0). We simulate the stock prices moving forward. At each intermediate time step, we use a neural network to guess the Delta (Z_t) based on the current stock prices. We update our running estimate of the option value along the path using these Deltas and the simulated market moves. When we reach the end of the option's life (T), we compare our final estimated option value with the actual payoff. If our initial guess or our neural network's Deltas were rubbish, there will be a massive gap. We then use backpropagation to adjust the initial price guess and the neural network's weights to minimise this gap across thousands of simulated paths. Once trained, Y0 is your fair price, and the neural networks have learned the perfect hedging strategy along the way.
The Finance Use Case: Non-linear XVA

This is not just an academic exercise. In the real world, banks have to calculate XVAs (Valuation Adjustments for credit, funding, and capital costs). Because these adjustments depend on the portfolio's value and the counterparty's default probability, they introduce nasty non-linearities into the pricing equations. Deep BSDE solvers allow quant desks to price and hedge these massive, multi-asset portfolios with complex funding constraints in a matter of minutes, bypassing the grid entirely.
Under the Hood: A PyTorch Sketch

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class BSDECell(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim, hidden_dim):
        super().__init__()
        # Neural network to approximate Z_t (the Delta) at a specific time step
        self.net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(input_dim, hidden_dim),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden_dim, input_dim)
        )
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.net(x)

class DeepBSDESolver(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_assets, num_steps, dt, hidden_dim=64):
        super().__init__()
        self.num_assets = num_assets
        self.num_steps = num_steps
        self.dt = dt
        # Learnable initial price Y0 and initial Delta Z0
        self.Y0 = nn.Parameter(torch.tensor([1.0]))
        self.Z0 = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(num_assets))
        # A network for each intermediate time step
        self.cells = nn.ModuleList([
            BSDECell(num_assets, hidden_dim) for _ in range(num_steps - 1)
        ])
    def forward(self, X_paths, dW_paths):
        batch_size = X_paths.shape[0]
        Y = self.Y0.expand(batch_size, 1)
        Z = self.Z0.expand(batch_size, -1)
        for t in range(self.num_steps):
            dW_t = dW_paths[:, t, :]
            # Simplified non-linear driver (e.g., representing funding costs)
            f = -0.05 * Y
            # Update Y using the Euler scheme for the BSDE
            Y = Y - f * self.dt + torch.sum(Z * dW_t, dim=1, keepdim=True)
            # Update Z for the next step
            if t < self.num_steps - 1:
                Z = self.cells[t](X_paths[:, t+1, :])
        return Y
How to Use This in an Interview or at the Pub

If you are chatting with a quant recruiter or a senior trader, drop this in when discussing multi-asset pricing or risk management. You can say: 'While standard Monte Carlo is the default for linear multi-asset options, it struggles with non-linearities like funding costs or default risk because you cannot easily do backward induction. Deep BSDE solvers get around this by framing the pricing PDE as a forward-backward SDE, using neural networks to learn the optimal hedging strategy along simulated paths. It basically turns a high-dimensional PDE problem into a standard deep learning optimisation task.' It shows you understand both the deep mathematical structure of quantitative finance and how modern machine learning is actually deployed on top-tier desks.
The Catch

Before you try to replace your entire library with neural networks, there are a few caveats. First, standard Deep BSDE is designed for European-style payoffs. Extending it to American or Bermudan options (where you have early exercise) requires solving an optimal stopping problem at each step, which makes training significantly more unstable. Second, because the update of the option value is sequential (like a Recurrent Neural Network), errors in the neural network's Delta approximations can accumulate over the simulation paths, leading to high variance. Finally, unlike a finite difference grid, Deep BSDE only gives you the price at a single starting point; if the spot market moves significantly, you have to retrain the model or use more complex parametric architectures.

sections.title: One Article or Paper Worth Reading: The Sins of Financial LLMs

content.text: If you have spent any time looking at financial LLM research over the last couple of years, you have probably seen some eye-watering claims. Models predicting stock moves with 80% accuracy, trading agents printing double-digit Sharpe ratios, and algorithms that seemingly possess a crystal ball. But if you try to run these in production, they have a funny habit of falling flat on their face. A stellar team of quantitative finance and AI heavyweights—including Stefan Zohren from the Oxford-Man Institute of Quantitative Finance and Alejandro Lopez-Lira (the academic behind the famous ChatGPT stock-forecasting paper)—have published a paper that explains exactly why: 'Evaluating LLMs in Finance Requires Explicit Bias Consideration' (arXiv:2602.14233).
Why This One Matters

This is not just another academic paper; it is a massive, highly necessary cold shower for the City. Right now, funds and banks are rushing to deploy LLMs for trading, research, and portfolio management. But they are evaluating them using standard machine learning metrics that completely ignore the classic, brutal biases of quantitative finance. This paper bridges that gap, showing how easy it is to build an LLM that 'time travels' in a backtest, and provides a concrete framework to stop yourself from losing real money in production.
The Five Sins of Financial LLMs

The authors reviewed 164 financial LLM papers published between 2023 and 2025 and surveyed 112 practitioners. They found a shocking lack of methodological rigour, identifying 'The Five Sins' that contaminate almost all reported financial LLM performance:

items: 1. Look-Ahead Bias (Time Travel): This is the big one. It happens when an LLM uses information that was not historically available at decision time. This occurs via 'parametric leakage' (the model was pre-trained on data up to 2024, but you are backtesting it on 2023 data, so it already knows how the story ends) or 'external RAG leakage' (retrieving articles that were updated post-event). Shockingly, only 26.8% of papers even mentioned this.

2. Survivorship Bias (The Ghost Companies): Evaluating an LLM on a static universe of currently active companies (like today's S&P 500) while ignoring the companies that went bankrupt, got acquired, or delisted along the way. Only 1.2% of the 164 papers controlled for this. If your model only tests on survivors, of course it looks like a genius.

3. Narrative Bias (The Illusion of Understanding): LLMs are designed to be coherent storytellers. They will generate a beautifully logical, highly persuasive rationale for a trade that is completely unsupported by the actual evidence available at the time. It masks complexity with fluent waffle. Only 11.6% of papers addressed this.

4. Objective Bias (The Confident Guess): Standard LLMs are optimised for next-token likelihood and aligned via human preferences, which rewards them for looking confident. In finance, knowing when to say 'I don't know' or 'No trade' is the difference between survival and ruin. LLMs structurally hate abstaining, preferring to hallucinate certainty. Only 12.2% of papers tackled this.

5. Cost Bias (The Paper Millionaire): Assuming zero execution friction. A strategy might look incredibly profitable on paper, but if you ignore transaction fees, slippage, and the 1.5-second latency it takes for the LLM to generate a response, it will bleed cash in the real world. Only 28.0% of papers accounted for this.

content.text: The Solution: The Structural Validity Framework
To save us from our own backtests, the authors propose a strict 'Structural Validity Checklist' built on five pillars:

items: Temporal Sanitation: Enforcing strict non-anticipativity. You must prove your model's pre-training cutoff is before your backtest starts, and your RAG system must use archived, point-in-time snapshots with verifiable timestamps.
Dynamic Universe Construction: Defining a time-indexed tradable universe that includes the dead, the merged, and the bankrupt.

Rationale Robustness: Treating explanations as testable objects. Run 'entity substitution' tests (e.g. swap company names to see if the model relies on its memory of what actually happened rather than the text provided) to ensure the logic holds up.
Epistemic Calibration: Forcing the model's action space to include 'No Trade' or 'Abstain' as legitimate options, and scoring it accordingly.
Realistic Implementation Constraints: Factoring in the exact distribution of generation latency, executing trades at the post-latency price, and deducting token costs and fees from your net returns.

content.text: Key Takeaways

items: Most academic papers claiming LLM trading outperformance are fundamentally flawed and functionally undeployable.
If you are building an LLM-based system, you are probably leaking future data into your model without realising it.
Evaluating an LLM requires a completely different set of tools and rigour than evaluating a standard quantitative model.

content.text: Quotes Worth Noting
"Finance-specific biases can inflate performance, contaminate backtests, and make reported results useless for any deployment claim."
"These biases break financial tasks in distinct ways and they often compound to create an illusion of validity."
What to Skim vs. What to Read

Skim the literature review breakdown and the details of the practitioner survey (Section 4). Focus your energy entirely on Section 2 (the detailed breakdown of the Five Sins) and Section 3 (the Structural Validity Framework). If you are writing code, head straight to Appendix C for the exact checklist template.
How This Connects to You

If you are a quant or developer building these systems, this paper is your shield. It stops you from presenting a backtest to your PM that looks like a money-printing machine, only to get found out when it blows up in production. If you are a PM or on the buy-side evaluating vendor tools, this paper is your sword. It gives you the exact, highly technical questions to ask vendors to see if their 'AI-driven alpha' is just a glorified look-ahead bias.
What to Say at the Pub or in the Office

Next time someone in the office brags about their new LLM-based sentiment trading strategy, ask them: 'How are you handling parametric knowledge leakage? If your model was pre-trained on a corpus that extends past your backtest start date, you are essentially letting your model read tomorrow's Financial Times before placing today's trade.'

Or, if you are reviewing a vendor: 'What is the average generation latency of your agent, and did you execute your backtest trades at P_t or P_{t+latency}? Because a 2-second delay in a fast-moving market will eat your paper alpha for breakfast.'
Our Take

This is the most important paper on financial AI published this year. For too long, the financial LLM space has been a playground for computer scientists who do not understand market microstructure or backtesting hygiene. By bringing the rigorous discipline of quantitative finance to LLM evaluation, Zohren, Lopez-Lira, and the team have provided a massive public service. Read it, print the checklist, and keep your models honest.

content.text: The "Everyone Else is an Idiot" Bias (Naïve Realism)

Have you ever noticed how, in the City, anyone who takes more risk than you is a reckless cowboy, and anyone who takes less is a bureaucratic hand-wringer? The late comedian George Carlin captured this beautifully: "Have you ever noticed that anybody driving slower than you is an idiot, and anyone going faster than you is a maniac?" In psychology, this isn't just a funny quirk; it’s a foundational cognitive bias known as Naïve Realism.

Coined by Stanford psychologist Lee Ross, naïve realism is our deep-seated, subconscious belief that we see the world objectively, exactly as it is. We assume that our opinions are the result of cold, hard, rational analysis of the facts. Consequently, we expect any reasonable, open-minded person who is presented with the same facts to reach the exact same conclusion.

When they don't, naïve realism dictates that we don't question our own perspective. Instead, we assume the other person must be uninformed (they just don't have the right data yet), lazy or stupid (they have the data but lack the brainpower), or biased (they are blinded by their personal incentives, ideology, or role).
The Classic City Standoff

You see this play out every single day in the tension between the Front Office (revenue generators) and Risk/Compliance. The Deal Team thinks: "This acquisition is a clear strategic win. The risk team is just being deliberately difficult and bureaucratic because they don't understand how the market actually works." Meanwhile, the Risk Team thinks: "This deal is a ticking time bomb. The deal team are reckless cowboys who only care about their immediate bonuses and are ignoring obvious red flags because they are biased."

Both sides genuinely believe they are the only ones looking at the situation "objectively". The deal team thinks Risk is stupid or lazy; Risk thinks the deal team is corrupt or blinded by greed. In reality, both are looking at the exact same transaction through entirely different "construals"—shaped by their distinct professional training, daily incentives, and institutional responsibilities. Trying to resolve this by simply throwing more "objective facts" at each other is like trying to put out a fire with petrol. The more you try to "enlighten" them, the more they see you as biased and stubborn.
How to Use It

First, in negotiations and meetings: When you hit a brick wall with a colleague or client, stop trying to win the argument by repeating your points. As Harvard behavioural scientist Julia Minson points out, the default human reaction to disagreement is to try and persuade the other person they are wrong, which almost always backfires. Instead, explicitly state your desire to learn. Try saying: "This is how I’m looking at the numbers based on X, but I know you’re coming at this from a different angle. What am I missing here?" This disarms their defensive "naïve realist" reflex and reframes the conversation from a battle of "who is right" to a collaborative puzzle.

Second, the ultimate interview cheat code: When an interviewer asks you: "Tell me about a time you had a conflict with a colleague or stakeholder. How did you handle it?" Most candidates give a generic answer about "communication" or "finding a compromise." You can do much better. Explain that you diagnosed the conflict as a classic case of naïve realism: "We were stuck because both teams believed they were the only ones looking at the data objectively. I realized that simply presenting more data wasn't working because they viewed my data as biased, and I viewed theirs as overly cautious. So, I sat down with them to map out how our different roles and incentives shaped how we interpreted the same facts. Once we acknowledged our different 'lenses', we were able to find a middle ground." This shows a level of psychological literacy and commercial maturity that will make any VP or MD sit up and take notice.
One Line to Remember
They aren't necessarily stupid or biased; they are just looking at the world through a different camera angle.
